evidence: Dilla's own Akai MPC3000 Limited Edition (one of 2,000 made in 2000) was donated by his mother, Maureen Yancey, to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture in 2014 (object 2014.139.1). Collaborators have described him as working largely with quantisation switched off. That working description is secondhand, while the instrument itself is documented.

trackPair.whatToListenFor: A quantise setting moves every drum hit onto the nearest point of a grid, so a beat stays perfectly even. Listen to 'Fall in Love' with that in mind. The kick drums do not land where a grid would put them: some come early, some late. The beat seems to stagger and yet it grooves, because the unevenness repeats. That is a person refusing the machine's correction on the machine itself.

explanation: Samplers like the MPC3000 can snap every drum hit exactly onto the beat, a setting called quantise, designed to make programmed rhythm correct. J Dilla usually switched it off and placed hits a bit early or a bit late by feel. His drums sound like they are leaning or tripping, but they still groove. With the 303 and Phuture, it is the classic case on this map of someone working against what a machine was meant to do. Musicians who played real drums started copying it, so the feel moved back into live playing, the drummers of the Soulquarians circle being the usual example. His use of the instrument is documented, and those who worked with him describe the unquantised method. His own MPC3000 is now in the Smithsonian museum in Washington.
